reading.rtitle: Why Nobody Quits in the Hard Month
paras: People almost never give up a language in the difficult first weeks. They give up around the third month, when nothing appears to be happening any more, and the reason is arithmetic rather than character. At the start you learn the things you use twenty times a day, so every new piece shows up immediately and the change is impossible to miss. Later the same amount of learning is spread across things that appear once a week, and the progress is identical while the evidence almost disappears.

That is what a plateau is, and the word is badly chosen, because it sounds like a flat surface and it is not. Nothing has stopped. What has changed is how often the improvement gets a chance to show itself. This is also why memory is a bad instrument here: it keeps the two conversations that went badly and quietly deletes the twenty ordinary ones that went fine, and after a month of that, a person who has improved is certain they have not.

The way out is not motivation, it is measurement. Pick one thing that is small and countable, record it on the same day every week, and compare it only with yourself. Two long silences instead of six is measurable; feeling more confident is not, and the second one cannot be defended to anybody, including you. And when the number does stop moving, that is the moment to name a single gap and spend the next month on it, rather than doing a little more of everything and calling it effort.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- B1 reading, written for this lesson from the published literature on language-learning plateaus and self-assessment

listenings.text: The first six weeks always feel fast, and there is nothing mysterious about why. At the beginning you are learning the things you use twenty times a day, so every single piece shows up immediately and you can feel it. Then people hit what they call a plateau, usually around the third month, and they arrive in my office convinced that they have stopped improving. They have not. What has happened is that the learning has moved to things that come up once a week instead of twenty times a day, so exactly the same amount of progress is now spread across far fewer moments. Nothing stopped. It just became much harder to see, and that is a completely different problem. So my advice is always the same and it is not about motivation. Keep track of one thing that is small and countable, on the same day every week, and compare it only with yourself. And do not trust your memory, ever. Memory keeps the two conversations that went badly and it quietly deletes the twenty that went fine, and after a month of that you will be certain you have gone backwards.

I recorded myself once a month for a year, two minutes each time, always the same kind of question. What I expected was that my vocabulary would grow, and honestly it barely did. If you put January next to December, the words are more or less the same words. What changed was the space between them. In January there are these long gaps where you can hear me looking for something, and by about August they are simply not there any more, and I never once practised that directly. The other thing I learned was accidental. There were two months when I did not record, because of work, and I fell behind and did not notice until the next recording, which was clearly worse than the one before it. That is when it stopped being a measurement for me and started being part of the method. The recording was not measuring the progress. It was causing some of it. And about listening to your own voice: it is horrible for about three recordings. After that you stop hearing yourself and you start hearing the sentences, and then it is just work.
